Could mortgage rates rise further? What bank packages in Singapore are signalling after Fed hike
article:
On Sept 16, the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023. Within days, Singapore banks pulled their fixed-rate packages, repriced them outside their usual schedule, and brought them back at higher rates.

So, will rates keep rising? No one can say for sure, but today’s bank packages offer a useful clue.

What bank packages are telling us

When a bank fixes your rate, it locks in its own funding cost for the same period.

What that costs depends on where the market expects Sora — the key interest rate benchmark for floating-rate home loans in Singapore — to go.

That’s why the difference between a bank’s three-year and two-year fixed rates, known as the spread, is worth watching.

If banks expect rates to rise, fixing for three years costs them more, so the three-year rate is priced higher and the spread widens. If they expect rates to stay stable, the spread stays narrow. And if they expect rates to fall, the three-year rate can even come in cheaper than the two-year rate.

Fixed rates have risen by 0.30–0.77 percentage points (refer to Table 1). For most home loans, the three-year rate is now slightly above the two-year rate. The exception is the $300,000 HDB loan, where the three-year rate is cheaper.

Things get more interesting, however, when we look at how the spreads have changed.

As Table 2 shows, the gap between three-year and two-year rates has narrowed for half of the packages. Where the spread has widened, the increase is small, at 0.12 percentage point or less.

This may indicate that rates could stay at this level for now or mildly rise, rather than climb sharply.

What the Fed is signalling

After raising rates in September, the Fed held them steady at its October meeting, but its latest statement leaves the door open to another rise.

About 76% of experts expect one more hike before the end of the year, according to CNBC's latest Fed Survey of fund managers, strategists and economists.

If that happens, expect the same pattern in Singapore as the previous time: Sora will likely move first. Whether fixed rates follow depends on how much of a higher Sora banks have already priced in.

Fixed rates are up 0.30 to 0.77 percentage points, and with the spread narrowing for half of the packages. This could indicate that banks expect rates to stay stable or rise only modestly from here.

These are indicators, not predictions. Fed projections can shift quickly, and banks can reprice their packages at any time. Treat this as context for your own decision rather than financial advice.

What has happened since the Fed hike

1. Sora moved before the Fed did.

Sora is the average rate banks charge each other to borrow Singapore dollars overnight, and most floating home loans are pegged to it.

Singapore rates tend to follow US rates because money moves freely in and out of the country, though the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s management of the Singapore dollar, and factors like large capital inflows, soften the link.

Banks also price in what they expect, so Sora started drifting up months before the Fed moved.

The monthly average Sora went from about 1.00% in April to 1.27% in August, and averaged about 1.34% in October. On a $500,000 floating loan, a 0.27 percentage point rise works out to roughly $110 a month more in interest in the early years.

2. Floating loans are still catching up.

Most floating loans use the three-month Sora — an average of daily Sora over the past three months — so it catches up with the daily rate slowly.

The three-month Sora hit a low of 1.02% on 29 April, was 1.20% the day before the Fed's announcement, and has reached 1.32% as at the time of writing (based on data as at Nov 9), 55 days later. If your loan is pegged to it, you're likely paying for the summer rise with a delay.

Singapore benchmark rates: Daily Sora and three-month compounded Sora:

3. Fixed packages were pulled, then repriced.

A fixed rate is a commitment: once it is agreed, the bank is stuck with it, even if its own costs rise.

So, after the Fed's move on Sept 16, banks withdrew packages first and repriced them after (see Table 3), according to Cashew’s internal bank package data.

What this could mean for you

If you're on a three-month Sora floating loan, expect the lag. The rise in the daily Sora is still feeding through the three-month average. Your rate won't jump sharply, but it may keep inching up for a few months, even if the headlines go quiet. If you're shopping for a fixed rate, treat pre-September rates as out of date. Packages have already been repriced higher, and many ads are still showing old rates. A rate isn't yours until it's approved. Packages are first come, first served, and they can change while your application waits in the queue. Don't panic. Over the life of your loan, rates will go up and down many times. If you switch to the lowest rate whenever your lock-in ends, you shouldn't overpay in the long run. You can do that by repricing (moving to a new package with your current bank) or refinancing (moving your loan to another bank).

The Fed’s September hike has already reshaped the market. Banks have repriced already, and Sora is still catching up.

But today's bank packages suggest rates may hold steady or rise only mildly from here, rather than climb sharply.

Whether you’re on a floating rate, coming to the end of a lock-in period, or buying your first home, what matters most is acting on current rates, not old ones. Compare your options early and make sure you’re on the lowest package available to you.

title: 4 Singapore Stocks I Would Buy if I Had S$30,000 to Spare
article:
Every investor with cash sitting on the sidelines asks themselves the same question: If I had fresh capital in my account today, where would I deploy it?
With S$30,000 ready to work in the Singapore market, swinging for the fences on a single stock is a fast track to striking out.
The smarter move is building a resilient, cash-generating portfolio designed to
compound
over time.
From steady dividend powerhouses to defensive market anchors, here are four core Singapore stocks to turn S$30,000 into a balanced, wealth-building engine.
How I Would Think About Allocating S$30,000
Putting S$30,000 into a single stock is like putting all your eggs in one basket: exciting when it works, but painful when it cracks.
I’d start with a steady
dividend
giant and a defensive grocery stock.
Those two are like a safety net, generating cash and holding steady if things get rocky.
Then I’d pick a proven market leader and a company with potential for a strong comeback.
That way, I get the chance for real growth without taking a risk on my whole stack.
This approach transforms S$30,000 into a well-rounded, wealth-building portfolio that can keep growing year after year.
DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05) — The Dividend Anchor
When building a cash-generating portfolio, every investor needs an undeniable core heavyweight.
DBS Group serves as the primary income engine, anchoring the portfolio with reliable payouts, high return on equity, and steady earnings visibility.
As Southeast Asia’s largest bank, DBS continues to deliver strong profits, driven by its expanding wealth management franchise, where assets under management reached a new high of S$544 billion in 3Q2026.
DBS offers a strong baseline annual dividend backed by its 9M2026 performance, where net profit reached a record S$8.82 billion.
On top of its S$0.66 ordinary quarterly dividend, DBS currently pays a S$0.15 quarterly capital return dividend, although this is a time-limited programme rather than permanent income.
Supported by a 39% cost-income ratio and a strong Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio of 15.9%, DBS is well placed to keep producing steady cash flow even when broader equity markets trade sideways.
Singapore Exchange Limited (SGX: S68), or SGX — The Structural Growth Leader
Building long-term wealth requires capturing secular trends, and SGX Group sits right at the center of Asia’s financial engine.
As Singapore’s main stock exchange, SGX operates an enviable regulatory moat with multi-asset expansion across currencies, commodities, and cash equities.
In FY2026, net revenue surged 13.9% to S$1.478 billion while adjusted net profit, which excludes one-off items, jumped 24.6% to S$759.5 million.
Reported net profit rose 7.8% to S$698.4 million.
Growth is driven by surging multi-asset volumes. Foreign exchange (FX) headline average daily volume expanded 33.1% to US$190.2 billion, while Securities Daily Average Value (SDAV) leapt 34.9% to S$1.8 billion.
Supported by government liquidity initiatives and high capital efficiency, SGX raised its regular dividend to S$0.445 per share and proposed a one-off S$0.125 additional dividend.
That would take total FY2026 dividends to S$0.57 per share, up from S$0.375 in FY2025.
Backed by guided medium-term revenue growth of 6% to 8%, a position in SGX delivers a high-margin compounding engine designed to expand capital over time.
Sheng Siong Group Ltd (SGX: OV8) — The Defensive Blue Chip
When market turbulence strikes, defensive blue chips steady the portfolio ship, and Sheng Siong Group stands out as a prime example of operational resilience.
As one of Singapore’s leading grocery chains, with 96 stores across Singapore and Kunming, China, its business model is anchored to everyday essentials that generate sticky, predictable demand through all economic cycles.
In 1H2026, revenue surged 11.9% year on year (YoY) to S$855.4 million, while net profit rose 11.9% to S$81.0 million, propelled by four new store openings and an expanded gross profit margin of 31.8%.
What sets Sheng Siong apart is its bulletproof balance sheet: the group has no bank borrowings and held S$402.3 million in cash as at 30 June 2026.
This fortress cash position supports an increased interim dividend of S$0.0375 per share, up from S$0.0320 a year prior.
An allocation in Sheng Siong adds steady income and defensive qualities to the portfolio.
SATS Ltd (SGX: S51) — The Opportunity Play
Rounding out the four picks, SATS Ltd adds real upside potential through its post-acquisition operational recovery.
After acquiring Worldwide Flight Services, SATS became a global aviation services group, operating over 225 stations across 27 countries.
That scale is starting to pay off as global air cargo volumes keep growing.
In 1QFY2027, group revenue expanded 11.3% YoY to S$1.68 billion, while net profit rose 6% to S$75.1 million.
Growth was fuelled by a 12.8% surge in Gateway Services revenue to S$1.33 billion, as cargo volumes handled rose 8.6%, outpacing the global market benchmark.
While near-term geopolitical costs and fuel prices keep margins under pressure, SATS continues securing new contract wins with major airlines like
Singapore Airlines
(SGX: C6L) and Air France-KLM.
For investors, SATS offers long-term earnings upside as its cash flows strengthen.
What I Would Avoid
Capital preservation matters just as much as growth.
Don’t put all your money into one sector, or you’ll leave yourself wide open to sudden industry shocks.
Also, don’t just follow the
hottest stocks
without digging into what those businesses actually do.
In the end, consistent discipline always outperforms quick thrills in investing.
Get Smart: Build a Portfolio, Not Just a Stock Pick
If you’ve got S$30,000 to invest, use it wisely to build a portfolio with purpose.
Don’t waste energy searching for that one “perfect” company.
Stick to companies with strong fundamentals, and give your investments time to grow.
It’s all about how you put your money to work, not just where you put it.
Imagine a life where steady income flows, no matter the market.
Our new free report, “Retire Early with Dividends,” reveals how. We’ve pinpointed 5 dependable Singapore dividend stocks that offer a proven, stress-free path to financial freedom. Stop just dreaming and start building your early retirement plan today. Your free guide awaits

for the latest investing news and analyses!

title: Climate investing’s next challenge: Identifying the companies ready to transition
article:
A portfolio can become cleaner on paper without the companies in it becoming any better prepared for a lower-carbon economy. Investors are increasingly weighing not just how much companies emit, but how well they can adapt and what that means for long-term investment risks and opportunities.

The distinction matters in a region where energy, manufacturing and other emissions-intensive industries play important economic roles. Companies with high emissions today may be investing heavily to transform their operations, while those with smaller carbon footprints are not necessarily better prepared for future policy, technology and market changes.

This approach is already taking shape in institutional portfolios. In 2025, Aware Super, one of Australia’s largest superannuation funds with more than A$235 billion ($210.84 billion) in assets, adopted a transition-based carbon reduction benchmark developed with MSCI for more than A$50 billion in public equities, bringing companies’ transition progress alongside their existing emissions into its investment framework.

“The industry has moved beyond portfolio optics to capital allocation with intent,” says Shane Edwards, head of Asia Pacific at MSCI. “Rather than simply excluding higher-emitting companies to lower a portfolio’s reported carbon footprint, investors are staying invested in companies with a credible path to lower emissions, because that is genuinely where engagement and capital can shift outcomes.”

Lowering a portfolio's reported emissions and investing in companies that are decarbonizing are not necessarily the same thing.

Some of the largest opportunities for emissions reductions lie in industries with the highest carbon footprints. Excluding these companies outright can mean overlooking businesses making credible progress.

But identifying them is not straightforward. Corporate targets alone reveal little about whether companies have the plans, resources or ability to deliver on their commitments.

That distinction is influencing how some institutional investors approach climate benchmarks.

“A company's current carbon footprint only tells part of the story,” says Agnes Hong, head of public market equities at Aware Super. “We wanted an approach that also captures where a business is heading and whether management is taking credible steps to position the company for a lower-carbon economy.”

The challenge is not simply deciding which companies are better prepared for the transition. It is determining how those assessments should affect portfolio weights without compromising diversification, risk controls or investment objectives.

“The transition to a lower-carbon economy will require significant change across many industries,” Hong says. “A forward-looking framework allows us to recognise companies making credible progress, even when they operate in sectors that have traditionally been viewed as emissions intensive.”

Singapore’s regulatory expectations are evolving along similar lines. Transition planning guidelines issued by the Monetary Authority of Singapore in March 2026 call on banks, insurers and asset managers to strengthen their forward-looking assessments of transition and physical risks, alongside engagement with investee companies.1

The implications extend to portfolio construction. More detailed assessments of companies’ transition readiness can inform investment decisions, but changes to benchmark weights can also affect sector exposures, diversification and tracking error. Asset owners face the task of balancing these considerations with their investment mandates and long-term performance objectives.

“Members expect us to take climate risk seriously, but they also expect us to remain disciplined investors,” says Hong. “Any climate framework we adopt must be capable of being implemented at scale, measured rigorously and justified through the lens of long-term member outcomes.”

The challenge becomes more complex across large portfolios managed by multiple investment teams. Consistent data, transparent methodologies and governance are essential to applying climate considerations without materially altering a portfolio's underlying risk and return characteristics.

“The market is already pricing transition risk, whether investors are ready for that or not,” says Edwards. “We have seen real repricing as capital moves toward companies with business models built for the transition, not simply those with the best-stated climate targets.”

Transition readiness is only part of the picture. Physical climate hazards can also affect company operations, supply chains and asset values, introducing risks that may not be apparent from company-level disclosures.

For Southeast Asian investors, this is particularly relevant given the region's concentration of manufacturing facilities, ports and infrastructure exposed to floods, extreme heat and severe storms.

Understanding where these risks are concentrated can help investors assess companies' capacity to adapt and strengthen resilience across regional and global supply chains.

“Location-specific insight is increasingly important for investors trying to get a real read on physical risk, which doesn’t live at a company’s headquarters, but wherever that company actually operates: the factory, the port, the warehouse,” says Edwards.

MSCI tracks 4.5 million operational locations across 780,000 companies against 31 physical climate hazards. Combining geospatial data with AI and other analytical techniques can help investors assess exposures that broader company-level measures may miss.

“Wildfires, floods and severe storms are already disrupting operations today, with an estimated US$1.3 trillion ($1.66 trillion) in financial exposure on the table,” Edwards says.

Such analysis can reveal where climate-related disruptions could affect individual businesses and how those exposures accumulate across a portfolio. It can also inform decisions about risk management, diversification and capital allocation.

Investors now have more information to assess not only where companies stand on emissions, but how prepared they are for the transition and the risks that could affect their operations.

“Setting climate goals is relatively straightforward,” says Hong. “The real challenge is translating those goals into portfolio construction decisions across tens of billions of dollars of assets while maintaining consistency, transparency and investment discipline.”

Aware Super's experience illustrates what that takes. Reliable data, robust methodologies and coordination across investment teams to incorporate climate considerations while managing diversification and tracking error.

For institutional investors, climate considerations cannot sit apart from the wider investment process. The growing availability of forward-looking data offers a more informed basis for assessing which companies are adapting, where risks remain and how those assessments should influence portfolio allocations.

The next phase of climate investing is not simply about meeting emissions targets, but using those insights to make investment decisions that account for both the risks of transition and the opportunities in companies helping to drive the region’s next phase of economic growth.

1Monetary Authority of Singapore, “MAS Sets Supervisory Expectations on Financial Institutions for Transition Planning Practices in Addressing Environmental Risk,” March 5, 2026.

For more on how MSCI and Aware Super worked together to develop a transition-focused benchmark, read the full story here.

title: Softbank, Grab and PETROS lock in US$1.85 bil seed capital for AI infrastructure in Malaysia
article:
KUALA LUMPUR (Nov 9): Petroleum Sarawak Bhd (PETROS), SoftBank Group Corp and Grab Holdings Ltd have entered into a joint development agreement (JDA) for US$1.85 billion in initial combined seed capital to develop AI infrastructure in Sarawak and Peninsula Malaysia.

Building on the framework agreement signed in Kuching, Malaysia, on Oct 8, 2026, the JDA marks the next phase of the partnership to advance plans to develop AI infrastructure in the nation.

Of the proposed initial investment of US$1.85 billion, US$1 billion will be invested in Sarawak and the other US$850 million in Peninsula Malaysia.

Of the US$1 billion earmarked for Sarawak, US$800 million is from SoftBank Group, US$750 million from Grab and US$100 million from PETROS. Meanwhile, SoftBank Group and Grab will invest US$650 million and US$200 million, respectively, for the project in the Peninsula.

The proposed investment will be deployed in stages, subject to projects achieving key development and customer contract milestones, and the necessary closing conditions.

The partnership combines SoftBank Group's global AI and technology capabilities, Grab's digital and AI expertise, and PETROS' local energy and infrastructure development experience.

See also: Asian stocks to rally on US tech surge, oil slump

The collaboration aims to build towards a long-term target of five gigawatts of AI compute capacity and will also explore opportunities across the wider AI value chain, including AI compute and services, advanced technologies, robotics, local workforce and community development.

"The investment forms part of a multi-year plan to develop AI compute capacity in Sarawak, and the parties will also seek additional investors and hyperscaler customers to support the project's development and long-term expansion," according to a joint statement on Monday.

The proposed investment will be deployed in stages subject to projects achieving key development and customer contract milestones, and the necessary closing conditions.

See also: Stocks climb as buyers step in despite Nvidia woes

SoftBank Group is the majority shareholder of the Sarawak AI project, with an option for Grab to increase its stake in future—reducing SoftBank Group's share while it remains the majority shareholder.

Grab will lead development of the Peninsular Malaysia project as a founding shareholder, with future funding expected through third-party equity and non-recourse project financing.

Given the parties' mutual interest in developing the AI ecosystem in Malaysia, SoftBank Group has agreed in principle to a five-year lock-up in respect of Grab shares that will be held directly by an entity within SoftBank Group, with the lock-up to take effect in accordance with the agreed terms and subject to customary exceptions.

Once fully operational, the facilities are expected to be among the largest AI infrastructure of their kind in Asia, and the project will be developed in close collaboration with Malaysia's federal government and the Sarawak government, aligning with the National AI Action Plan 2026–2030 and Sarawak's Post Covid-19 Development Strategy 2030.

Through the Sarawak Gas Roadmap, PETROS is advancing critical gas infrastructure to strengthen Sarawak's energy security and support its industrial expansion.

As the master developer of the Kuching Low-Carbon Hub, PETROS is also building an integrated low-carbon industrial ecosystem that brings together upstream development, carbon capture solutions, LNG-to-power, downstream processing, industrial parks, gas terminals and deep-sea port infrastructure.

Sarawak's abundant energy resources, established power generation capacity and growing digital economy ambitions provide a strong foundation for the development of large-scale AI infrastructure.

These investments will support Malaysia's ambition to become a regional AI hub, while creating opportunities for Sarawak to diversify its economy and move towards higher-value industries.

title: Stocks climb as buyers step in despite Nvidia woes
article:
(Nov 10) : A renewed wave of dip buying drove stocks to their best day since April in the wake of a technology selloff that had roiled Wall Street, with the market also gaining as oil prices sank.

Following a drawdown in one of the world’s most-crowded trades, a gauge of chipmakers jumped almost 7%. The S&P 500 rose 2.35%. The Nasdaq 100 added 3.4%. That’s despite a 4.3% slump in Nvidia Corp. amid an investigation into Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang after his admission of an affair with a woman identified in a series of reports as a suspected Chinese spy.

“For now, the market is showing the resilience needed to turn last week’s weakness into another buying opportunity,” said Mark Hackett at Nationwide. “That’s an encouraging sign.”

Also helping sentiment was a drop in energy costs on optimism around efforts to end the Iran war. President Donald Trump struck a more conciliatory tone, saying it’s “highly unlikely” he will order extensive strikes on the Islamic Republic.

That helped reduce anxiety about inflation ahead of a report on consumer prices — the last before the Federal Reserve meeting in December. Still, 10-year Treasuries fell amid gains in riskier assets.

“We continue to see economic conditions as supportive of corporate fundamentals,” said Brock Weimer at Edward Jones. “Thus, we recommend that investors maintain an overweight allocation to equities relative to fixed income.”

See also: Asian stocks brace for selloff as AI rout deepens

The sharp deterioration in momentum that played out in equities last week may have pushed investor pessimism close to peak levels, according to JPMorgan Chase & Co. strategists led by Dubravko Lakos-Bujas.

The recent tech selloff represented a reset rather than the start of a structural downturn in the AI investment cycle. But the rebound does not remove the risks created by concentrated positioning and elevated expectations, said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi at UBS Chief Investment Office.

While it’s unlikely last week shut the door on volatility, what unfolded may have been more about investors repositioning within the AI trade rather than abandoning it altogether, noted Chris Larkin at E*Trade from Morgan Stanley.

See also: S&P 500 sinks 4% as AI washout rattles Wall Street

“There’s good reason to believe the stock market’s long-term rally is intact, especially given that the selloff overshadowed another week of strong economic data,” he added.
